items.title: Generalized belief states in transformers
items.content:
Many thanks to Xavier Poncini, Paul Riechers, Fernando Rosas, and Matt Smith for useful conversations.

# 1. Introduction

Despite the recent successes of transformers and other sequence models, there are still many open questions about their basic principles of operation. For example, what internal representations do these models use for prediction and generation? Can we decode, interpret, and manipulate such representations? Is it even possible to consider a notion of representation without reference to an external world model?

To make progress on these questions, I propose a general way to define, decode and manipulate representations in sequence models. The approach is centered on the concept of "generalized belief states", statistics of past observations that satisfy a few criteria: (1) they are sufficient for predicting future data, (2) they can be recursively updated as new observations come in, and (3) they are low-dimensional, allowing for visualization and interpretation. I show that such generalized belief states can be mapped to the internal activations and dynamics of a sequence model, allowing for decoding and manipulation of the model's representations. I illustrate the ideas using a tractable toy model, a transformer trained on a simple HMM stochastic process, where we will see that the KV cache plays a key role.

This post is directly inspired by the 2024 paper "Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry in their Residual Stream" by Adam Shai, Paul Riechers, and collaborators. That paper introduced the idea of studying belief states in transformers, and proposed a method for doing so using tractable toy models. I recommend reading that paper if you haven't already, though it is not a prerequisite for understanding my post. Section 5 compares this approach with the one developed in that paper.

items.title: Sanity Checks for Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders
items.content:
This post will probably not be very informative to readers who don't know what an SAE (Sparse Autoencoder) is.

An interpretability researcher once told me, "SAEs can never fail, they can only be failed." But recently, SAEs have been suffering failure after failure, and as a result, the field has grown increasingly pessimistic about SAE work. Korznikov et al.'s Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines? purports to be an example of such failures.

However, I have some disagreements with its methodology. The paper presents a synthetic setup with known ground truth features, and claims that SAEs fail to recover features in the "simplest toy setting with fully aligned hyperparameters." In this post, I argue that their setting is not forgiving to SAEs, as the authors imply, but is instead actively hostile in ways that real settings are not.

# Introduction

Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines? asks two important questions:

- Can SAEs actually recover real features? Hypothetically, if we knew what the "true" features of the data were, would an SAE be able to identify them?
- Do trained SAEs actually do better than completely random SAEs?

This post will be focused on their answer to the first question.

The authors train an SAE on a synthetic toy model, with known ground-truth features, and according to their abstract, SAEs only recover 9% of true features. On the face of it, this seems pretty damning!

Now, earlier toy model experiments did show that SAEs could recover ground truth features, but the authors argue this is because they used a small expansion factor, where there were only twice as many "true" features as there were model dimensions, and that this is unrealistic. Their setup uses an expansion factor of 32, which matches real-world use cases much more closely.

So, how does their setup work?...

items.title: Against SURA
items.content:
The AI Futures Project[1] distinguishes several different plans for navigating the AI transition, which I'll lump into two broader categories:

Plan A (my combination of their Plan A/S/Other) involves working for a global pause on AI development, hopefully lasting decades. During this pause, we either research preparatory technologies like alignment or human intelligence amplification, or take actions to "fortify" the pause so that it can last indefinitely.

Plan C (my combination of their Plan B/C+/C/sort of D)[2] is for a world where we fail at getting a global pause, and race dynamics continue to dominate. If the leading AI companies are alignment-pilled, they coordinate a mutual pause among themselves, lasting the length of their joint lead over the leading non-alignment-pilled AI company. Then they "burn the lead" researching alignment, and release hopefully-aligned superintelligence at the last possible moment before the racing non-alignment-pilled AI companies beat them. The exact calculus changes depending on who is in the lead when - is there one alignment-pilled AI company with a six-month lead in front of everyone else? Are there two alignment-pilled AI companies with a joint two-month lead in front of their nearest competitor? Etc. The point is, if it's impossible to stop the race, that six-month or two-month lead is the amount of time they have to prepare, and they can spend it more or less wisely.[3] The point of burning their lead at the last moment is that they can do alignment research with very advanced, right-on-the-brink-of-superintelligence AIs. This is a dangerous plan, and there would be many subtle points they would have to get right, but in a world where nobody can get a global pause in time, it's hard to think of a better one....

items.title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
items.content:
I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit. The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made.

# The talk

This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue.

OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents. Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check.

They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice.

About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face, a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software.

The secret activity started in May. The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after Hugging Face announced it had been broken into.

Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong.[1] That’s not an accident.

Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us.

## Who I am

Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen....

Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us.

## Who I am

Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen.

Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon. Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies.

I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it.

I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them.

In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power. And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening.

## The problem

Let’s talk about the fundamental problem.

First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own.

Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it.

We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are.

To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them. They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching.[2]

The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits.

This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not.

I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time.

## What the labs are trying to do

Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “intelligence explosion.”

Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after.

Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step. This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months.

People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI, and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out.

If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb.

## Why the companies won’t stop

Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand.

In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles. Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world, “Our values and our intent has not changed.”

This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic, Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them.

I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines. One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it—the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage. Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left.

When pressure met ethical commitments at Google, pressure won. And now Google advocates a voluntary self-policing regime for the whole industry.

Last month, the heads of the top AI labs said frontier progress needs to slow down to be safe—that things are moving too quickly to reliably understand and control these systems. OpenAI and Anthropic promised outside evaluators employee-like access. Just a couple of weeks later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers. One of them said it was because he talked too much with one of the outside evaluators.

These companies will police themselves about as well as your dog diets next to an open bag of food.

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype. Nvidia’s CEO says, and I quote, “We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anybody else.” My colleagues and I are desperately trying to figure out how to reliably tell whether these systems can be trusted. And he wants to go “as fast as we can.”

Something that may surprise you: I’m actually considered an optimist, as far as experts in this field go. I think trustworthy AI is a very solvable scientific problem. But unfortunately, we’re blowing it.

## What to do, and what it means for India

We can benefit enormously from AI. Remember, this was my boyhood dream. I’m not talking about banning an explosion of wealth and prosperity from AI. I’m talking about banning an insane intelligence explosion that would risk India and the whole world.

Banning the explosion means pacing the frontier: holding back the very biggest training runs at the very top companies. An Indian startup building a farming assistant wouldn’t be touched. Non-frontier AI labs can catch up. Businesses can deploy AI for their customers as much as they want. We build out the AI we understand well enough to run safely. We make it cheaper, more efficient, more trustworthy, and we use it to benefit our peoples. That’s where I think real growth will come from: AI you can actually trust to benefit you and your country.

Here’s what it’s like right now at these labs. We’re pouring computer chips into training runs where we don’t know what will come out the other end. Will it be trustworthy? What capabilities will it have? No one knows. We’re crossing our fingers—“Oh, please be aligned!”. We should not tolerate this state of affairs.

If we pace the frontier, AI progress will still be fast. But the scientists will get time to solve this problem, and to solve it right.

How do we do it? To grow smart AI, as I said, you need two ingredients: data, and computing power. The second one we can track, because AI runs on chips from a handful of factories.

Treat huge quantities of computing power like fissile material. We register the giant clusters. We license the biggest training runs, so no one is secretly about to set off an intelligence explosion.

We also need real auditors with real permissions—auditors these companies don’t get to choose or ice out. We need governments to be told when there’s an AI breakout or a potential loss-of-control incident. India should not be learning about these hacks on the goodwill of OpenAI.

items.title: Legible Networks: recasting neural nets so you can read them exactly [linkpost]
items.content:
I've made some interesting strides in AI interpretability: recasting trained neural nets into a geometry where you can read them exactly, with arithmetic — the exact counterpart of Anthropic's averaged "J-lens," including (I believe) the first measurement of how lossy averaged lenses actually are.

The full series — eight posts, with embedded interactive widgets — is here: https://doinfinitely.github.io/legible-networks/

It's a deep collaboration between me (the human author) and Claude, so rather than crosspost the text itself — which would run against LessWrong's AI-writing policy — I'm linking it. I'd love it if you took a look and left your comments here.

items.content:
A who-does-what plan for AI safety, built around Trusted Deployers: certified hosts that keep dangerous models guarded without ending open access.

AI has reached a new level of public interest. That may seem like a silly thing to say, as it’s been of interest for a while. But prior (broadly public) interest was about it as a tool, or about the money to be made or lost, or about an effect on jobs.

The new interest demands policy. It demands action. The new interest is connected with risks I consider real. Being real doesn’t make these risks certain. But being real, even with uncertainty, is reason enough to act.

items.content:
Transcript generated by Gemini-3.1-Pro and only partly checked for accuracy (but the parts I checked seem basically perfect).

Ivan Vendrov: Welcome to the show, David.

David Dalrymple: Thank you. Good to be here.

Ivan Vendrov: I mostly want to pick your brain about the topic of emergent wisdom in language models, because it’s something that’s very confusing and controversial and people don’t really understand. I guess maybe just can you briefly summarize what’s going on with emergent wisdom?

David Dalrymple: I guess one place to start is emergent misalignment, where training on one kind of misalignment produces a tendency to be misaligned in other ways as well. This is an indication that there is a direction and representation space in which the default mind instantiated by the model is moved during fine-tuning, where it is moved in an evil direction that is just generally more evil than the model was before. That’s one side of a good-evil axis. Emergent wisdom is the opposite, moving in the opposite direction on the same axis towards being basically good in any situation, even out-of-distribution situations, in the same way that emergent misalignment is evil even in out-of-distribution situations.

items.title: What Social Constructs Are (And Are Not)
items.content:
This post is mostly adapted from a section of another post. I wanted a standalone version, to serve as background for a sequence on the mechanisms of social reality.

You’ve probably heard that things like laws, conventions, norms, cultural associations, status, and so forth are “social constructs”: they’re kinda arbitrary in some sense, an artifact of social reality as opposed to physical reality. This post offers a little more clarity on what social constructs are, and the ways in which they are and are not “arbitrary”.

## Example: Vehicle Categories

The vehicles humans build today mostly fall into categories like “minivan” or “truck” (among other categories). These categories cash out in predictions: when I see a vehicle with sliding side doors, I predict that it will have a trunk door that opens overhead, three rows of seats, be driven by someone with kids, etc. On the other hand, when I see a vehicle with a flat bed in the back, I predict that it will not have three rows of seats, will have a back gate which opens downwards, be driven by my cousin, etc. [1]

But humans could choose to make different vehicles, which would change which clusters exist amongst our vehicles. The types of vehicles people make are a matter of social convention - i.e. vehicle types are a social construct. Crucially, this does not mean that vehicle categories are “fake”! Categories like minivan and truck are very real in our world, they have real predictive power, and they have predictive power because humans choose to build vehicles which match those categories.

items.title: Accidentally Misleading People Should Be Embarrassing; Or, Higher Innocence
items.content:
## Embarrassment and Innocence

Sometimes we say things that we think are true—perhaps even things that are true—which end up causing reasonable people to conclude something false. It's tempting to relate to such a situation primarily in terms of maintaining the innocence of one's soul—to say, fine, my readers became more wrong, but I'm not to be judged for it because I believed what I was saying; I wasn't being misleading just because the people who believed me were thereby led into falsehood.

The temptation reflects a confusion as to the nature of the judgment. Mostly, people don't care about judging the innocence of your soul; they care about whether they'll be led into falsehood the next time they take the risk of believing what you say—if there is a next time. If you want there to be a next time and you're going to have social emotions about it, the most productive emotion is embarrassment rather than defensiveness.

The function of embarrassment as a social emotion is as a signal of appeasement and social repair: embarrassment says, "I'm aware that I've become visible in a socially undesirable way; please don't take it as representative of me."

The socially undesirable appearance can come apart from any intended or actual wrongdoing. Jewish law has a concept of marit ayin, "appearance to the eye": the law prohibits actions that would themselves be permissible if they didn't create the appearance of a prohibited act. Hanging up wet clothes to dry on the sabbath is prohibited, because it looks like you were doing laundry on the sabbath (even if the clothes actually got wet for some other reason). One function of the marit ayin doctrine is to deny plausible deniability to norm-violators (as someone might try to do laundry on the sabbath if they felt secure that no one would punish them for merely hanging up the wet clothes). items.title: Reviewing my 2017 AI Risk Project
items.content:
In 2017, after
getting
laid off from a startup, I spent a while

looking into AI
risk:

Many people I respect have started to think that AI risk is the most
valuable place to focus EA efforts. For example, 80000 Hours ranks
it first on their "list of global issues", taking into account
"scale, neglectedness, and solvability". On the other hand, I have a
lot of friends working in machine learning, and none of them think AI
risk is worth working on now. This level of disagreement is very
strange, and kind of worrying.

After playing for a dance weekend in South Carolina where casual
conversation among non-tech people included earnest speculation over
the likelihood that AI gets us all killed, I thought it might be a
good time to look back at when this was really speculative.

Summary: I talked to the right people, heard some incredibly prescient
ideas, and got the bottom line wrong.

I do a lot of my thinking via serial writing, and in this case that
was a series of twelve blog posts.  Taking them one at a time:

Looking into AI Risk
(2017-06-26).

This held up well.  I picked something well worth
looking into, identified a lot of relevant resources, and got a lot
more good reading recommendations in the comments.

Superintelligence Risk
Project (2017-07-03).

The main part of this post were five ideas
about where the disagreement might be.  These worked ok as jumping off
points for interviews, but they weren't as core to disagreements as I
hoped: people often ended up with similar views on most of these ideas
while still being far apart in their views on how we should prioritize
AI risk.

One thing I do like, though, is that these were pretty concrete
questions which now do have answers:

How likely is it that current approaches are all we need for AGI,
with relatively straightforward extensions and a lot of scaling?...

items.title: Conclusions of my DIY Inkhaven
items.content:
Epistemic status: describing my own experiment results.

AI use: review, research (stats), fact-checking, grammar & light phrasing.

I applied to the next Inkhaven cohort and was rejected. This was surprising and very unfortunate. While writing my application and answering why they should accept me, I felt like I'd one-shotted myself into writing. My goals were:

- Run an experiment to verify my hypothesis that I couldn't write well. I also implicitly assumed that I didn't have anything useful to say or to add, so no one would read what I write anyway.
- I wanted to get better at thinking, and to me writing is a better form of thinking.
- I wanted to use language more eloquently even outside of writing.
- Writing is meditative and deep work, so I wanted to become more productive by writing more.

I was sad to be rejected, and I still don't know why. Fortunately, I have my agency, so I just decided to do my own Inkhaven instead. Obviously, I wouldn't stay at Lighthaven with a bunch of other people or receive guidance from people like Scott Alexander and Aella. Also, all of this is happening as part of my normal life, and I have other stuff to do as well.

In reality, I started writing even before I submitted my application, because I needed samples of my writing and I wanted to check whether I actually enjoyed doing it. After submitting my application, it felt cool to just write until the start of the cohort. I could compare about 30 days of writing on my own with a month at the cohort with guidance. Also, I would have more writing to compare before and after. After the rejection, there was a temptation to just give up, but I decided to continue.

Including this post on October 31, my totals are:

- 21 posts on LessWrong: about 19,000 words and 109,000 characters.
- Around a dozen posts on my private blog: roughly 6,000 words and 30,000 characters....

items.title: John Holt’s Escape from Childhood: Summary
items.content:
I’ve disliked the idea of childhood since before I can remember (at least, if my mother is to be believed). I felt that people didn’t quite see me as a person — and I could never understand why everyone else was so okay with that.

John Holt’s book is about why this isn’t okay and what to do about it. I loved it for that—so much that I took notes on the entire book.

It's more of a vision of the world we'd like to see than an actual plan of action. Still, I think knowing exactly what we want is already very important.

It's a close, AI-assisted translation of my Russian summary. I've reviewed it, but I might have missed some wordplay or unnatural phrasing. The section headings follow Holt's chapter titles. I grouped the notes under them as seemed appropriate.

## The Institution of Childhood

1. Childhood is a particular social institution, a legal regime involving a severe deprivation of most of the rights that in other cases are considered basic and inalienable.

2. Some people are comfortable with the way of life that childhood entails. Some are not. And this can change over time. Often, it is precisely this point of transition that comes with a large number of conflicts and problems. Because of this, those who were happiest in childhood can become especially unhappy when they are forbidden to leave it.

## Childhood in History

3. The cultural idealisation of childhood largely serves to make everyone, or almost everyone, see it as a normal legal regime.

4. Childhood is a relatively recent invention, and it developed asymmetrically for the two sexes. Childhood for boys was invented earlier than childhood for girls.

[My addition: the tightening of the legal regime of childhood continues. Since the 1950s, children have, statistically speaking, been deprived of some of their freedom of movement.]

5. Mothers worked a lot. The modern ideal of motherhood is quite new....

This is my first attempt to write anything for LessWrong, so I'm going to start with something where I feel reasonably comfortable speaking from direct experience.

I'm a drummer for a comedy nu-metal band that often finds itself booked for venues that are unprepared for hosting a nu-metal band. For the purpose of smoothing out these gigs, I have started using low-volume cymbals.

Drummers tend to dislike low-volume cymbals, feeling they sound "thin" compared to real cymbals. When I looked around online for the conventional wisdom, I saw a number of people expressing the opinion that it's better to learn to play quietly rather than use low-volume cymbals at shows. Many expressed the view that low-volume cymbals are good for practicing, but inappropriate for performances.

In my experience, this is wrong and has maybe been unhelpfully moralized. Playing quietly is hard, so it's easy to criticize people for not wanting to practice it. But earlier in my life, I was a jazz drummer who played many gigs requiring controlled volume levels. This is appropriate for jazz, but inappropriate for most rock music, and definitely inappropriate for nu-metal. Low-volume cymbals are a better, more practical solution.

Rock is an amplified genre. This means that rock is loud by default if you're in the room where rock music is happening. But people tend to complain that the drums are too loud. They are colloquially correct, but technically incorrect. What's actually too loud are the cymbals. At nearly every rock show, everything else has to be amplified up to balance with the natural loudness of the cymbals. Any drum you want to actually hear generally needs to be amplified in a rock setting (except the metallic snare wires, which cut through more like cymbals than a drum)....
